The origins of the Hanseatic League can be traced back to the chaotic security landscape of Northern Europe following the collapse of the Carolingian Empire and the subsequent Viking incursions. As central authority weakened, German merchants and traders sought safety in numbers and mutual defense. The foundational moment is generally considered to be the establishment of the merchants' guild of Gotland, known as the *Gotlandfahrer*, who secured a charter from Henry the Lion, Duke of Saxony, in 1158. This charter granted the German merchants significant privileges in the port of Visby, a crucial hub on the trade route to the East. Simultaneously, the city of Lübeck was founded in 1143 by Count Adolf II of Holstein and later refounded by Henry the Lion in 1159. Lübeck’s strategic location, controlling the short land portage between the North Sea and the Baltic Sea, allowed it to become the central node where goods from the West could be transferred to ships bound for the rich eastern markets. During this formative period, the "Hanse" was not a political entity but a loose association of traveling merchants (*Kaufleute*) who shared a common legal code, the *Lex Mercatoria*, and traveled together in armed convoys
